edges.description: Knockout mice have normal retinal histology, normal photoreceptor and synaptic markers, and normal scotopic and photopic ERGs at 2 and 6 months.
edges.limitations: Retinal assessment stopped at 6 months, and the knockout cannot be used to study the human retinal mechanism. Why the mouse retina is spared is not known.

nodes.description: Scotopic (rod) responses are reduced or extinguished in most reported families, often becoming extinguished by late childhood.

evidence.reference_title: Cone-rod dystrophy and amelogenesis imperfecta (Jalili syndrome): phenotypes and environs.
evidence.snippet: Electrophysiologically, photopic flicker responses were impaired; scotopic responses were extinguished at the age of 10 years.

evidence.snippet: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) revealed atrophy of the outer retinal layers, and electroretinography (ERG) showed extinguished cone and rod responses.

nodes.description: Photopic (cone) responses are reduced or non-detectable.

nodes.description: Both primary and permanent dentitions are affected. Teeth are yellow-brown, sensitive and lose enamel rapidly after eruption. One compound heterozygous family included a parent with the retinal disease but no dental phenotype.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in CNNM4 cause Jalili syndrome, consisting of autosomal-recessive cone-rod dystrophy and amelogenesis imperfecta.
evidence.snippet: In all affected members of these pedigrees, the enamel of the primary and secondary dentitions was grossly abnormal and prone to rapid posteruptive failure, in part reflecting hypomineralization.

evidence.reference_title: Expanding the genotypic spectrum of Jalili syndrome: Novel CNNM4 variants and uniparental isodisomy in a north American patient cohort.
evidence.snippet: Three unrelated sporadic cases were systematically evaluated for ocular phenotype and determined to have cone-rod dystrophy with bull's eye maculopathy, photophobia, and nystagmus.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in CNNM4 cause Jalili syndrome, consisting of autosomal-recessive cone-rod dystrophy and amelogenesis imperfecta.
evidence.snippet: Using a positional-candidate approach, we have identified mutations in the CNNM4 gene, encoding a putative metal transporter, accounting for the condition in all seven families.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in CNNM4 cause recessive cone-rod dystrophy with amelogenesis imperfecta.
evidence.snippet: Using a genome-wide single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) haplotype analysis to fine map the locus and a gene-candidate approach, we identified homozygous mutations in the ancient conserved domain protein 4 gene (CNNM4) that either generate a truncated protein or occur in highly conserved regions of the protein.

evidence.reference_title: Identification of a mutation in CNNM4 by whole exome sequencing in an Amish family and functional link between CNNM4 and IQCB1.
evidence.snippet: Whole exome sequencing was then performed for the three affected individuals and identified a homozygous nonsense mutation (c.C1813T, p.R605X) in the cyclin and CBS domain divalent metal cation transport mediator 4 (CNNM4) gene located within the 2p14-2q14 Jalili syndrome locus.

evidence.snippet: No association was found between logMAR visual acuity and mutation domain (P=0.748).

nodes.description: Disease alleles include nonsense, frameshift, splice-site, large deletion and missense variants. Missense variants in the CBS domain reduce protein and mRNA stability and lower Mg2+ extrusion activity without mislocalizing the protein; other disease missense variants abolish Mg2+ extrusion in cultured cells.

evidence.reference_title: Mutations in CNNM4 cause Jalili syndrome, consisting of autosomal-recessive cone-rod dystrophy and amelogenesis imperfecta.
evidence.snippet: Nine mutations are described in all, three missense, three terminations, two large deletions, and a single base insertion.

evidence.reference_title: Basolateral Mg2+ extrusion via CNNM4 mediates transcellular Mg2+ transport across epithelia: a mouse model.
evidence.snippet: Imaging analyses revealed that CNNM4 can extrude Mg(2+) by exchanging intracellular Mg(2+) with extracellular Na(+).

evidence.reference_title: Basolateral Mg2+ extrusion via CNNM4 mediates transcellular Mg2+ transport across epithelia: a mouse model.

evidence.reference_title: Functional and pathogenic insights into CNNM4 variants in Jalili syndrome.
evidence.snippet: Our findings demonstrated that these variants exhibit significantly reduced protein stability and increased mRNA decay rates compared with wild type.

nodes.description: Progressive loss of cone and then rod photoreceptor function and structure, with cones more severely affected. Outer retinal layers thin on OCT. The only reported histopathology, from an enucleated eye of a 63-year-old woman, showed loss of photoreceptors, subretinal autofluorescent material, partly preserved inner retinal lamination, Muller glial disorganization and increased microglia. How CNNM4 deficiency injures photoreceptors is unknown.

nodes.description: Affected human enamel reaches about half the mineral density of normal enamel, retains amorphous organic matrix, and carries elevated magnesium with reduced calcium. Cnnm4 knockout mouse enamel has immature rods with raised magnesium and reduced calcium and phosphorus. The retained matrix may hinder the crystal growth of enamel maturation. Dentine is also undermineralized in human teeth.

nodes.description: CNNM4 is absent from secretory-stage ameloblasts and strongly expressed at the basolateral membrane of ruffle-ended maturation-stage ameloblasts, the same polarized position it occupies in intestinal epithelium, where it carries out transcellular Mg2+ transport. Its loss is proposed to prevent removal of Mg2+ from the maturing enamel compartment.
